card.name: Rieldans
card.tagline: Dust-raising ancient Khoisan courtship and animal dance
card.profile: Rieldans, also known as the Riel or Ikhapara by the Nama, is one of the oldest indigenous celebratory dance traditions of South Africa, historically performed by the San, Nama, and Khoi peoples around campfires. Characterized by rapid, dust-raising footwork described by the Afrikaans phrase 'Dans lat die stof so staan', the dance imitates animal courtship rituals and daily labor like sheep shearing and bread dusting. Dancers perform in vibrant working-class clothes to fast-paced music played on handmade tin guitars, violins, and accordions. Today, it thrives through revived regional and national competitions that preserve its unique blend of ancient Khoisan storytelling and later colonial musical influences.
card.insight: In July 2015, the Nuwe Graskoue Trappers from Wupperthal won 14 gold medals in Los Angeles dancing the ancient rieldans.
card.profile_long:
The Rieldans, historically known to the Nama as Ikhapara, represents one of the oldest indigenous dance forms in South Africa. Deeply rooted in the social, educational, and spiritual lives of the San, Nama, and Khoi peoples long before European arrival, the dance originally served as a celebratory ritual following successful hunts, good harvests, or community gatherings around a campfire. As Khoisan languages declined and Afrikaans became widespread among these communities, the dance adopted the name 'riel,' borrowed from the Scottish 'reel' during colonial interaction. In the mid-twentieth century, between the 1940s and 1950s, the riel evolved into a central form of entertainment for farmworkers and sheep shearers, particularly in the Northern Cape and Karoo regions.

The dance is distinguished by its frantic, energetic tempo and ingenious footwork designed to kick up sand, inspiring the famous Afrikaans expression 'Dans lat die stof so staan' (dancing at a fast and energetic pace resulting in a lot of dust). Dancers perform primarily in circles or small groups, enacting narrative scenes of courtship, animal behaviors, and rural work routines. Mimicry plays a central role; performers portray the movements of ostriches, meerkats, baboons, horses, and snakes. Courtship rituals feature bird-like flirting known as 'vlerksleep', where male dancers use a coat panel, raised arm, or brimmed hat to invite partners and court women.

Musically, the rieldans combines ancient Khoisan rhythms with Western colonial elements, accompanied by boeremusiek, Dutch folk melodies, and early American minstrel traditions. Musicians play unique handmade folk instruments, such as the 'ramkie'—a guitar crafted from an oil tin, wood, and strings—alongside accordions, mouth organs, hand-crafted violins, and banjos. Dancers wear bright, colorful costumes that evoke prancing animals while mirroring traditional working-class farm attire, with men frequently utilizing their hats as essential props to win a lady's hand.

To prevent the art form from dying out, the Afrikaanse Taal en Kultuurvereniging (ATKV) launched a formal preservation project in 2006, creating national championship competitions. This revitalization brought international recognition to the tradition, highlighted in July 2015 when the Nuwe Graskoue Trappers dance troupe and orchestra from Wupperthal competed at the World Championship of Performing Arts in Los Angeles, securing 14 gold medals in the senior dance category.

sections.origins_and_history: The riel is considered one of the oldest entertainment forms used as a social, cultural, and educational tool by the Khoisan people long before Western cultures arrived at the Cape of Good Hope. Originally danced by Khoisan hunters around campfires after hunting expeditions or harvests, it absorbed distinct Irish and Scottish folk music influences alongside Dutch folk songs. Over time, the native Khoisan languages mostly disappeared, and the Afrikaans word 'riel' was borrowed from the Scottish 'reel'. Between the 1940s and 1950s, it became the dance of working-class farmworkers and sheep shearers, especially in the Northern Cape and Karoo regions. In 2006, the Afrikaanse Taal en Kultuurvereniging (ATKV) launched the riel project to preserve the art form through national championships.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Danced at an energetic, frantic pace, the rieldans relies on intricate, fast footwork meant to kick up dust in the sand, giving rise to the phrase 'Dans lat die stof so staan'. Performed by groups often in a circle, the choreography consists of cultural gestures that tell stories of wooing, courtship, and daily labor. Dancers imitate animal and bird movements—such as the ostrich, butterfly, antelope, baboon, snake, meerkat, and strutting horses—using techniques like 'bokspring' (gamboling), trotting, and 'kapperjol'. Courtship involves 'vlerksleep' (bird-like wing-dragging), where a man uses his coat panel, arm, or hat to court a partner. Occupational moves depict sheep shearing, horse galloping, and the 'askoek' slap, where a dancer places the right foot above the left knee and slaps it to demonstrate dusting excess ash from traditional ash-baked bread.
sections.music_and_instruments: Rieldans features lively music influenced by Irish and Scottish folk music, Dutch folk songs, minstrel tunes, and boeremusiek. Instrumentation combines traditional and handmade working-class instruments. Central to the sound is the 'ramkie', a tin guitar made out of an empty oil can, a piece of wood, and strings. Accompaniment also includes odd handmade violins, accordions, mouth organs, and banjos.
sections.costume_and_setting: The dance was traditionally performed in the dusty sand around a campfire, and modern competitive performances retain dusty floor settings to highlight the kicking up of dust. Costumes are bright and colorful to portray the prancing of animals, while reflecting traditional working-class farm clothes. For male dancers, the hat is a crucial accessory used during courtship gestures to win a lady's hand in marriage.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Originally danced during celebrations after hunting expeditions or good harvests, the rieldans acts as a narrative tool for romance, animal observation, and community solidarity. It portrays wooing and lovemaking through animal courtship rituals, as well as the daily working environment of sheep shearers, herdsmen, and farm laborers.
sections.notable_figures: The Nuwe Graskoue Trappers, a famous rieldans troupe and orchestra from Wupperthal, brought international prominence to the dance in July 2015 at the World Championship of Performing Arts in Los Angeles, winning 14 gold and eight silver medals in the senior dance category, alongside seven silver medals and an open dance trophy won by their musical band.
sections.regional_variants: The dance is known as Ikhapara by the Nama people, derived from the word 'khapas' meaning hat. It is strongly preserved across the Northern Cape and Karoo regions of South Africa.
sections.lineage: Originating from ancient Khoisan hunter-gatherer campfire traditions, the dance integrated Scottish and Irish reel elements and Western colonial instruments (guitar, violin) while maintaining traditional storytelling, animal mimicry, and working-class heritage.

claims.text: Riel (or Rieldans) is an Afrikaans word for an ancient celebratory dance performed by the San, Nama and Khoi.
The dance is known as Ikhapara by the Nama, derived from khapas meaning hat.
The Afrikaans expression describing the energetic pace resulting in dust is 'Dans lat die stof so staan'.
Everyday farm tasks like dusting ash from bread are manifested in the askoek slap.
In 2006 the ATKV launched the riel project to preserve the dance through championships.
In July 2015 the Nuwe Graskoue Trappers won 14 gold and eight silver medals in Los Angeles.
The rieldans is currently a living dance tradition.

movement_profile.footwork: Ingenious and frantic footwork designed to kick up dust ('Dans lat die stof so staan'), including trotting, strutting, and cross-knee leg positioning.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Mimicry of wings ('vlerksleep'), hat-holding, and hand-slapping the leg above the knee.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Dynamic movement imitating gamboling ('bokspring') and animal courtship poses.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Group performed in a circle around a campfire or dusty performance space.
movement_profile.partnering: Male and female courtship pair interaction using hat or coat props.

footage.description:
The Riel dance (Die Rieldans) is to the countryside in the Western Cape Province, what the "Kaapse Klopse" is to the urban coloured communities in Cape Town. 
The ritual of Riel dancing has it's roots in simple courtship stories that are reenacted by troups all over the "Swartland" area.
